title: Biological Techniques
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 200L practical/lab-methods curriculum: advanced microscopy (light vs electron), tissue fixation/sectioning/staining for histology, chromatography, centrifugation, spectrophotometry, pH and buffers, sterilisation and aseptic technique, culture media, and common quantitative lab techniques (hemocytometer counting, electrophoresis). Distinct from BIO107/BIO108 (introductory practicals) by focusing on instrumentation and preparative technique.

questions.question: Compared with a light microscope, a transmission electron microscope (TEM) achieves far greater resolution mainly because it:
options: Uses a beam of electrons, which have a much shorter wavelength than visible light
Uses ordinary visible light passed through more powerful glass lenses
Magnifies the specimen using sound waves instead of light
Requires no specimen preparation at all
questions.correct_answer: Uses a beam of electrons, which have a much shorter wavelength than visible light
questions.explanation: Resolution is limited by the wavelength of the imaging radiation; electrons have a much shorter wavelength than visible light, permitting resolution of much finer detail.

questions.question: A scanning electron microscope (SEM) is best suited for studying:
options: The detailed three-dimensional surface topography of a specimen
The internal ultrastructure of organelles within a thin cell section
Living cells in real time without any preparation
Colour differences between stained tissues
questions.correct_answer: The detailed three-dimensional surface topography of a specimen
questions.explanation: SEM scans a focused electron beam over a specimen's surface and detects reflected electrons, producing detailed three-dimensional surface images, unlike TEM which images thin internal sections.

questions.question: Because electron microscopy requires the specimen chamber to be under vacuum, a major limitation of electron microscopy is that it cannot be used to:
options: Observe living, unfixed specimens
Achieve high resolution
Study cell ultrastructure
Examine surface features of a specimen
questions.correct_answer: Observe living, unfixed specimens
questions.explanation: The vacuum and electron bombardment required for electron microscopy would kill and dehydrate living cells, so only fixed, dehydrated, non-living specimens can be examined.

questions.question: In histological technique, the first step after collecting a tissue sample, done to preserve cell structure and prevent decay, is:
options: Fixation, for example in formalin
Staining with haematoxylin and eosin
Sectioning with a microtome
Mounting in resin on a slide
questions.correct_answer: Fixation, for example in formalin
questions.explanation: Fixation cross-links proteins and halts autolysis and bacterial decay, preserving tissue architecture as close to the living state as possible before further processing.

questions.question: Before a fixed tissue block can be cut into thin sections with a microtome, it must first be embedded in a supporting medium such as:
options: Paraffin wax
Distilled water
Liquid nitrogen only
Concentrated iodine
questions.correct_answer: Paraffin wax
questions.explanation: Embedding infiltrates the dehydrated tissue with paraffin wax, giving it firm, uniform support so very thin sections can be cut without tearing.

questions.question: In the standard haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining procedure used in histology, haematoxylin stains cell nuclei:
options: Blue/purple, because it binds acidic components such as DNA
Pink, because it binds cytoplasmic proteins
Green, because it reacts with lipids
Colourless, since haematoxylin does not bind nuclear material
questions.correct_answer: Blue/purple, because it binds acidic components such as DNA
questions.explanation: Haematoxylin is a basic dye that binds acidic (basophilic) structures such as nucleic acids in the nucleus, staining them blue-purple, while eosin (acidic) stains cytoplasm pink.

questions.question: A microtome is a laboratory instrument used to:
options: Cut very thin, uniform sections of embedded tissue for microscopic examination
Separate cell components by density using centrifugal force
Measure the absorbance of a coloured solution
Sterilise glassware using high pressure and temperature
questions.correct_answer: Cut very thin, uniform sections of embedded tissue for microscopic examination
questions.explanation: A microtome uses a precision blade to slice embedded tissue blocks into sections thin enough (a few micrometres) for light to pass through under a microscope.

questions.question: Chromatography is a laboratory technique used mainly to:
options: Separate a mixture of substances based on their differing movement through a stationary phase carried by a mobile phase
Measure the exact temperature at which a substance boils
Kill microorganisms present in a solution
Determine the pH of an unknown solution
questions.correct_answer: Separate a mixture of substances based on their differing movement through a stationary phase carried by a mobile phase
questions.explanation: Chromatography separates components of a mixture according to their differential affinities for a stationary phase (e.g. paper) versus a moving solvent (mobile phase).

questions.question: In paper chromatography, the retention factor (Rf value) of a substance is calculated as:
options: The distance travelled by the substance divided by the distance travelled by the solvent front
The distance travelled by the solvent divided by the distance travelled by the substance
The total time taken for separation to occur
The mass of the substance divided by the mass of the paper
questions.correct_answer: The distance travelled by the substance divided by the distance travelled by the solvent front
questions.explanation: Rf is defined as the ratio of the distance moved by a solute spot to the distance moved by the solvent front, and is used to help identify substances.

questions.question: Centrifugation separates components of a mixture (for example, cell organelles in a homogenate) primarily on the basis of their:
options: Density and size, which determine how fast they sediment under centrifugal force
Electric charge only
Colour
Solubility in organic solvents
questions.correct_answer: Density and size, which determine how fast they sediment under centrifugal force
questions.explanation: Centrifugal force accelerates sedimentation, and denser or larger particles sediment faster and at lower speeds than smaller, less dense ones, enabling differential centrifugation.

questions.question: In differential centrifugation of a cell homogenate, increasing the centrifuge speed progressively causes organelles to sediment in which general order?
options: Nuclei first (lowest speed), followed by mitochondria, then microsomes/ribosomes at the highest speed
Ribosomes first, followed by nuclei, then mitochondria
All organelles sediment simultaneously regardless of speed
Mitochondria first, followed by nuclei, then ribosomes
questions.correct_answer: Nuclei first (lowest speed), followed by mitochondria, then microsomes/ribosomes at the highest speed
questions.explanation: Because sedimentation rate depends on size and density, the largest structures (nuclei) pellet at low speed first, followed by progressively smaller organelles at higher speeds.

questions.question: A spectrophotometer is used in biological laboratories chiefly to:
options: Measure the amount of light absorbed by a solution at a specific wavelength, which relates to solute concentration
Separate a mixture into its individual components
Sterilise culture media before use
Measure the exact pH of a buffer
questions.correct_answer: Measure the amount of light absorbed by a solution at a specific wavelength, which relates to solute concentration
questions.explanation: A spectrophotometer quantifies light absorbance of a sample, which, via the Beer-Lambert relationship, can be used to estimate the concentration of a coloured solute.

questions.question: In spectrophotometry, a 'blank' solution (e.g. solvent with no analyte) is run before measuring samples in order to:
options: Zero the instrument so absorbance readings reflect the analyte alone, not the solvent or cuvette
Increase the sensitivity of the instrument permanently
Sterilise the cuvette
Calibrate the wavelength dial only
questions.correct_answer: Zero the instrument so absorbance readings reflect the analyte alone, not the solvent or cuvette
questions.explanation: The blank accounts for any absorbance contributed by the solvent, cuvette, and instrument itself, ensuring later readings represent only the substance of interest.

questions.question: The pH scale is a measure of:
options: The concentration of hydrogen ions in a solution
The concentration of dissolved oxygen in a solution
The total dissolved solid content of a solution
The temperature of a solution
questions.correct_answer: The concentration of hydrogen ions in a solution
questions.explanation: pH is defined as the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration, indicating how acidic or alkaline a solution is.

questions.question: A buffer solution used in biological experiments functions to:
options: Resist changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added
Increase the pH of a solution rapidly and permanently
Sterilise the solution against microbial growth
Increase the solution's electrical conductivity
questions.correct_answer: Resist changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added
questions.explanation: A buffer, typically a weak acid and its conjugate base, neutralises small additions of acid or base, keeping pH relatively stable, which is essential for enzyme and cell studies.

questions.question: Autoclaving, a common method of sterilising laboratory media and equipment, works by using:
options: Steam under pressure at a high temperature (commonly 121 degrees Celsius) to kill microorganisms including spores
Ultraviolet light exposure for a few seconds
Freezing the equipment to below zero degrees Celsius
Soaking equipment in distilled water overnight
questions.correct_answer: Steam under pressure at a high temperature (commonly 121 degrees Celsius) to kill microorganisms including spores
questions.explanation: An autoclave uses pressurised steam, typically at 121 degrees Celsius for about 15-20 minutes, to destroy all microbial life including resistant bacterial endospores.

questions.question: Working near a Bunsen burner flame while inoculating culture media is a practice intended primarily to:
options: Create an updraft of hot air that reduces the chance of airborne contaminants settling onto the sterile media
Sterilise the entire laboratory room
Increase the temperature of the culture media
Provide light for easier observation
questions.correct_answer: Create an updraft of hot air that reduces the chance of airborne contaminants settling onto the sterile media
questions.explanation: The rising hot air current around a lit Bunsen burner helps carry airborne contaminants away from the immediate work area, supporting aseptic technique.

questions.question: A nutrient agar plate that has been properly sterilised but shows microbial growth after incubation with no deliberate inoculation indicates:
options: Contamination, meaning aseptic technique was not properly maintained
Successful, expected experimental results
That the agar was too concentrated
That the incubator was too cold
questions.correct_answer: Contamination, meaning aseptic technique was not properly maintained
questions.explanation: Growth on an uninoculated, sterile control plate signals contamination from the environment, equipment, or technique, invalidating the assumption of a pure culture.

questions.question: Agar is widely used as a solidifying agent in microbiological culture media mainly because it:
options: Remains solid at typical incubation temperatures and is not readily digested by most microorganisms
Provides all the nutrients microorganisms need to grow
Is a strong antibiotic that prevents bacterial growth
Changes colour to indicate the pH of the medium
questions.correct_answer: Remains solid at typical incubation temperatures and is not readily digested by most microorganisms
questions.explanation: Agar melts at high temperature but resolidifies and stays solid at incubation temperatures, and few microbes can metabolise it, making it an ideal inert gelling agent.

questions.question: A culture medium that supplies only the basic nutrients needed for general microbial growth, without favouring any particular organism, is called:
options: A general-purpose (basal) medium
A selective medium
A differential medium
An enriched medium only
questions.correct_answer: A general-purpose (basal) medium
questions.explanation: A basal/general-purpose medium supports growth of a wide range of non-fastidious organisms without selecting for or against particular species.

questions.question: A selective culture medium is designed to:
options: Encourage the growth of certain organisms while inhibiting the growth of others
Support growth of every organism equally
Change colour to distinguish between species
Provide no nutrients so only spores survive
questions.correct_answer: Encourage the growth of certain organisms while inhibiting the growth of others
questions.explanation: Selective media contain agents (e.g. antibiotics, dyes, extreme salt) that suppress unwanted organisms while permitting growth of the target group.

questions.question: The streak plate method is a technique used in microbiology mainly to:
options: Obtain isolated, single colonies from a mixed microbial culture
Measure the exact number of cells in a suspension
Stain bacterial cell walls for Gram classification
Extract DNA from bacterial cells
questions.correct_answer: Obtain isolated, single colonies from a mixed microbial culture
questions.explanation: Progressive dilution of the inoculum across streaks on an agar plate spreads out cells so that, after incubation, well-separated single colonies (each from one original cell) can be picked.

questions.question: A haemocytometer is a specialised counting chamber used in the laboratory to:
options: Estimate the number of cells (such as blood cells or yeast cells) per unit volume of a suspension
Measure the pH of blood samples
Separate plasma from blood cells
Determine the molecular weight of a protein
questions.correct_answer: Estimate the number of cells (such as blood cells or yeast cells) per unit volume of a suspension
questions.explanation: A haemocytometer has an etched grid of known volume under the coverslip, allowing a cell count within the grid to be converted into cell concentration per millilitre.

questions.question: When counting yeast cells with a haemocytometer, cells that sit exactly on the boundary lines of a counting square are conventionally counted by:
options: Including cells touching two designated sides (e.g. top and left) and excluding those touching the other two
Counting every boundary cell twice
Excluding all boundary cells from every square
Including all boundary cells regardless of which sides they touch
questions.correct_answer: Including cells touching two designated sides (e.g. top and left) and excluding those touching the other two
questions.explanation: A consistent rule (commonly, count cells touching the top and left boundaries, ignore those on the bottom and right) avoids double-counting or omitting boundary cells.

questions.question: Gel electrophoresis is used to separate molecules such as DNA fragments or proteins mainly on the basis of:
options: Size (and charge), as they migrate through a gel matrix under an electric field
Colour under white light
Their solubility in ethanol
Their boiling point
questions.correct_answer: Size (and charge), as they migrate through a gel matrix under an electric field
questions.explanation: In an electric field, charged molecules move through the porous gel at rates that depend on their size and charge, with smaller fragments generally migrating faster.

questions.question: In agarose gel electrophoresis of DNA, samples are loaded into wells at the end of the gel nearest the:
options: Negative electrode (cathode), since DNA is negatively charged and migrates toward the positive electrode
Positive electrode, since DNA is positively charged
Centre of the gel, regardless of charge
Either end, since charge is irrelevant to loading position
questions.correct_answer: Negative electrode (cathode), since DNA is negatively charged and migrates toward the positive electrode
questions.explanation: DNA's phosphate backbone carries a net negative charge, so samples are loaded near the cathode and migrate through the gel toward the anode.

questions.question: A dye such as ethidium bromide (or a safer modern alternative) is added to a DNA gel or the DNA sample in order to:
options: Bind to the DNA and fluoresce under ultraviolet light, making the separated bands visible
Increase the speed at which DNA migrates through the gel
Sterilise the DNA sample
Convert double-stranded DNA into single strands
questions.correct_answer: Bind to the DNA and fluoresce under ultraviolet light, making the separated bands visible
questions.explanation: Intercalating dyes bind between DNA base pairs and fluoresce under UV light, allowing the otherwise invisible separated DNA bands to be visualised and photographed.

questions.question: Serial dilution, a technique frequently used before plating a microbial sample, is performed to:
options: Reduce the cell concentration stepwise so that colony counts on a plate are practical to count accurately
Increase the total number of microorganisms present
Sterilise the microbial sample completely
Change the genetic composition of the microorganisms
questions.correct_answer: Reduce the cell concentration stepwise so that colony counts on a plate are practical to count accurately
questions.explanation: Serial dilution lowers an overly concentrated sample by a known factor at each step, so that a countable number of colonies (typically 30-300) appears after plating and incubation.

questions.question: When calculating the total number of viable bacteria in an original sample from a diluted plate count, the formula used is:
options: Colony forming units counted multiplied by the total dilution factor, divided by the volume plated
Colony forming units counted divided by the total dilution factor
Colony forming units counted multiplied by the volume plated only
The dilution factor alone, ignoring the colony count
questions.correct_answer: Colony forming units counted multiplied by the total dilution factor, divided by the volume plated
questions.explanation: Viable count (CFU/mL) equals the number of colonies counted, multiplied by the reciprocal of the dilution used, divided by the volume of diluted sample plated.

questions.question: In tissue processing for light microscopy, dehydration of the fixed tissue through a graded series of increasing alcohol concentrations is necessary because:
options: Water must be removed before the tissue can be infiltrated with wax, which is not miscible with water
Alcohol stains the tissue for easier viewing
It sterilises the tissue completely
It increases the tissue's natural colour
questions.correct_answer: Water must be removed before the tissue can be infiltrated with wax, which is not miscible with water
questions.explanation: Paraffin wax embedding requires a water-free tissue, so a graded alcohol series gradually replaces water without causing the shrinkage or distortion of an abrupt change.

questions.question: A calibrated glass instrument used to measure and transfer precise, small, variable volumes of liquid in the laboratory is a:
options: Pipette
Beam balance
Bunsen burner
Microtome
questions.correct_answer: Pipette
questions.explanation: Pipettes (graduated, volumetric, or micropipettes) are designed to accurately measure and dispense specific liquid volumes, essential for reagent preparation and dilutions.

questions.question: An analytical/beam balance used in the laboratory to determine the mass of a chemical reagent should be:
options: Placed on a stable, level surface and tared (zeroed) before each new measurement
Used only while liquids are actively boiling nearby
Tilted to one side to increase reading precision
Loaded with reagents before it is switched on or zeroed
questions.correct_answer: Placed on a stable, level surface and tared (zeroed) before each new measurement
questions.explanation: Accurate weighing requires a stable, vibration-free, level surface, and taring removes the mass of any container so only the sample mass is recorded.

questions.question: The Gram staining technique classifies bacteria into two broad groups mainly based on differences in their:
options: Cell wall structure and peptidoglycan content
Rate of reproduction
Ability to move using flagella
Colour under natural light without staining
questions.correct_answer: Cell wall structure and peptidoglycan content
questions.explanation: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall that retains crystal violet stain, while Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer and outer membrane that loses the stain and take up the counterstain instead.
